verses.text: Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the children of Israel. No one went out, and no one came in.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and the mighty men of valor.
All of your men of war shall march around the city, going around the city once. You shall do this six days.
Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the ark. On the seventh day, you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets.

It shall be that when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, and when you hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people shall shout with a great shout; and the city wall shall fall down flat, and the people shall go up, every man straight in front of him.”
Joshua the son of Nun called the priests, and said to them, “Take up the ark of the covenant, and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams’ horns before Yahweh’s ark.”
They said to the people, “Advance! March around the city, and let the armed men pass on before Yahweh’s ark.”

It was so, that when Joshua had spoken to the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams’ horns before Yahweh advanced and blew the trumpets, and the ark of Yahweh’s covenant followed them.
The armed men went before the priests who blew the trumpets, and the ark went after them. The trumpets sounded as they went.
Joshua commanded the people, saying, “You shall not shout, nor let your voice be heard, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout.”
So he caused Yahweh’s ark to go around the city, going about it once. Then they came into the camp, and stayed in the camp.
Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up Yahweh’s ark.

The seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams’ horns in front of Yahweh’s ark went on continually, and blew the trumpets. The armed men went in front of them. The rear guard came after Yahweh’s ark. The trumpets sounded as they went.
The second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. They did this six days.
On the seventh day, they rose early at the dawning of the day, and marched around the city in the same way seven times. Only on this day they marched around the city seven times.
At the seventh time, when the priests blew the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, “Shout, for Yahweh has given you the city!
The city shall be devoted, even it and all that is in it, to Yahweh. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, she and all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.
But as for you, only keep yourselves from what is devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted it, you take of the devoted thing; so you would make the camp of Israel accursed, and trouble it.
But all the silver, gold, and vessels of brass and iron, are holy to Yahweh. They shall come into Yahweh’s treasury.”

So the people shouted and the priests blew the trumpets. When the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight in front of him, and they took the city.
They utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, both young and old, and ox, sheep, and donkey, with the edge of the sword.
Joshua said to the two men who had spied out the land, “Go into the prostitute’s house, and bring the woman and all that she has out from there, as you swore to her.”

The young men who were spies went in, and brought out Rahab with her father, her mother, her brothers, and all that she had. They also brought out all of her relatives, and they set them outside of the camp of Israel.
They burned the city with fire, and all that was in it. Only they put the silver, the gold, and the vessels of brass and of iron into the treasury of Yahweh’s house.

But Rahab the prostitute, her father’s household, and all that she had, Joshua saved alive. She lives in the middle of Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers, whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.

Joshua commanded them with an oath at that time, saying, “Cursed is the man before Yahweh, who rises up and builds this city Jericho. With the loss of his firstborn he will lay its foundation, and with the loss of his youngest son he will set up its gates.”
So Yahweh was with Joshua; and his fame was in all the land.

footnotes.content: Jericho heard what happened at the Jordan and bolted every gate. The text says no one went out and no one came in — a whole city holding its breath behind stone. Fear always mistakes a wall for safety, and I have prayed that prayer myself, barring the door against a God who was already being kind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the tense: not 'I will give' but 'I have given.' Before a single foot marched, the outcome was already settled in God's mouth. Joshua is handed a promise and then told to walk it out; that is usually the order of things with the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One lap a day for six days, no battering rams, no siege towers — just an army walking a slow circle in the dust. The Lord often asks for the kind of obedience that looks foolish from a distance and feels tedious up close. Jericho watched them go by and did not know what was being built in the walking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days — the number of completeness runs through the whole procession. These were rams' horns, the shofar, the same rough instrument that called Israel to worship and to war. God's plan for that wall was not a weapon but a sound, carried by men walking in step with His ark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wall falls at a shout, not a strike. Hebrews 11:30 remembers it plainly: by faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. Faith here is not a feeling but a seven-day habit of walking where God said to walk.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua does not improvise; he repeats what he was told, down to the number of priests and the kind of horns. A leader's work, it turns out, is often just careful transmission. I have watched good shepherds do this — keep their hand on the words they were given and not on their own bright ideas.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The order of march tells the story: armed men in front, yes, but the ark at the heart of everything. Israel did not leave the presence of God back in camp while the soldiers went to work. Whatever we call our front line, the Lord means to be standing in the middle of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests blow, the ark follows, and no one can see the road ahead past the procession. The ark was the throne of God's presence, and it moved at walking pace. He does not outrun His people; He goes with them at the speed of their feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Armed men, then trumpeters, then the ark, then the rear guard — a strange parade with the treasure in the middle. The soldiers were not so much guarding the ark as the ark was covering them. I have known that arrangement to be true in my own small marches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua forbids a single word until the day he says to shout. Six days of silence is a long discipline for people who had just been promised a city. Some things must be carried quietly in the heart before they are said aloud, and God's timing is part of His gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One lap, and then back to camp, with nothing apparently changed — the wall still stands, the gates still shut. Most of the life of faith looks exactly like this: doing the thing again, and going home to supper. The Lord is not embarrassed by the uneventful day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Early in the morning, the ark is lifted again. There is something steadying in the repetitiveness of these verses — the same priests, the same horns, the same road. God's faithfulness meets us in the plain resumption of yesterday's obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The trumpets do not stop; the text says they blew continually. This was not a signal to begin but a sound that kept on, filling the air over the whole march. I think of how often I need a long unbroken reminder rather than one bright moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The second day, once around, and back to camp — and the writer keeps counting so that we feel the weight of six of these. Endurance is not glamorous, but it is where promises are usually received. Nothing in the text suggests the wall was cracking; only the obedience was compounding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the seventh day they start at dawn and go around seven times. Nobody explains the change mid-week; they simply do it. There comes a point where obedience stops calculating and starts keeping pace with the God who commands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the last blast Joshua finally releases the shout: 'Yahweh has given you the city!' The shout comes after the gift, not to earn it. Praise is the right sound to make when you realize you are standing on ground you did not win.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The city is put under the ban — herem, the Hebrew word for something set apart to God by destruction, taken out of ordinary use. Rahab and those in her house are the single exception, and the reason given is what she did for the spies. Judgment and mercy stand in the same verse; what I can say is that God noticed a kindness done to His messengers in a doomed place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Keep yourselves from the devoted thing — the warning is urgent because one man's private grab can make the whole camp 'accursed,' literally 'troubled.' The Hebrew verb here, akar, will attach itself to Achan in the very next chapter. Sin in a camp is never as private as it feels.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver, gold, bronze, and iron go into Yahweh's treasury instead of into anyone's tent. The firstfruits of a taken city belong to the One who gave it. It is a good early habit to ask what is genuinely the Lord's and what I am only holding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people shout, the trumpets sound, and the wall comes down flat — the Hebrew suggests it fell beneath itself. Then comes the strangest detail: they go up, each man straight ahead, no ladders, no breach to hunt for. God made a door where there had only ever been stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the hard verse, and I will not smooth it over. The whole city falls to the sword — old and young, man and woman, even the animals. I read it with fear and honesty, holding it beside Scripture's witness that the Judge of all the earth does right, and beside the scarlet cord in the same chapter. I have no tidy answer, only a deep need for mercy I did not earn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua remembers the oath two spies made to a Canaanite woman and sends those same men back for her. An oath made in a crisis is still an oath. The Lord keeps His covenant through the small faithfulness of people who could easily have forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rahab's whole household — father, mother, brothers, relatives — is brought out and set 'outside the camp of Israel.' That phrase is not an afterthought; under the law the unclean were placed outside the camp. She is saved first and brought near afterward, and the gospel has a familiar shape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They burn the city, and only the silver and gold and vessels go into the house of Yahweh. I notice that word 'only' — everything else in Jericho ended as ash. What is given to God outlives what is kept for ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rahab the prostitute — a Canaanite, a woman, a harlot — is written into Israel and remembered 'to this day.' Readers today hear an echo of that scarlet cord running through the story of grace: Matthew's genealogy names her as an ancestor of Jesus. As of 2026-10, I am still steadied that the Lord builds His line out of people others would have left outside the camp.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua binds the ruins with an oath: whoever rebuilds Jericho will pay for it with his sons. It is a solemn marker that this ground was not won by human engineering but given by God. Some things are better left as ruins than rebuilt on our own terms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chapter ends where it began, with God's word: Yahweh was with Joshua. The fame is a byproduct; the presence is the point. If I could leave one line in the margin of this whole strange, wonderful chapter, it would be that one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
